There’s no escaping the pair’s towering reputations, which turn out to be both a blessing and a trap. In this odd-couple comedy by Jen Silverman, Farrow and LuPone are cast as unlikely housemates in rural Iowa, lost souls eager to move on from their pasts.
Not even the ever-reliable director Jack O’Brien can get a firm grasp on this squiggly story, but at least he doesn’t have to make the effort alone: Who wouldn’t want Farrow and LuPone on their team?
But although the play’s scenario certainly sets them up for banter, the dialogue itself is bizarrely unambitious and often illogical.
The problem is that this version of “The Roommate,” working backward from that fact, delivers a pair of very satisfying performances that cancels out the play.
The two living legends – one a grand dame of American theater, the other a classic Hollywood star – are the only performers in, and reason to see, a just-fine play.
So my disappointment in the play is not due to some casualty of heart or humanity — the show’s got well-enough doses of both — but rather its missing sense of deeper purpose.
It may be given a glossy sheen and a smattering of good punch lines in The Roommate, but it sends us out into the night with the dull sensation of wondering what exactly we were clapping for.
With its affective writing and polished presentation, this Broadway incarnation succeeds as a thoughtfully entertaining star vehicle for Mia Farrow and Patti LuPone.
The Roommate is surprising, charming, and highly enjoyable with stand-out performances by its star-studded cast and a feel-good story that will have you smiling for the rest of your evening.
In truth, both characters learn from, and are to some extent liberated by, each other, and both stars make that education buoyantly entertaining.

It’s terrible to feel discarded — especially by one’s own children. In Jen Silverman’s comedy The Roommate, now at Broadway’s Booth Theatre, Mia Farrow and Patti LuPone play two very different women in similar predicaments. Sharon (Farrow) is a divorced 65-year-old housewife living in Iowa City.
Margo Martindale and Patti LuPone are both giving performances that are, in their different ways, exceptional, and watching them work together is a genuine pleasure.
Farrow’s quietly captivating performance makes The Roommate worth the stay.

There’s no show without the stars — their staccato interplay is expert — and while Silverman’s play often feels like it might evaporate through those beams, it’s nice to spend time with these two old friends.

Directed with his usual finesse by Jack O’ Brien and beautifully designed by Bob Crowley (who has created a spacious, airy Midwest farmhouse) and lit gorgeously by Natasha Katz, the play serves mostly as a showcase for the spectacular Mia Farrow (in a long-awaited return to the stage) and her real-life bestie, Patti LuPone, each of whom do their...
Farrow, in just her third Broadway outing in 50 years, is enchanting from start to finish.
At once clueless and brilliant, terrified of the unknown but fed-up with the familiar, Farrow’s Sharon is rich enough to pay the rent all on her own.

Of course, with Farrow and LuPone under the direction of six-time Tony Award winner Jack O’Brien, this is an occasion for cheering although this comedy drama, a cross between a female version of The Odd Couple and Breaking Bad is both predictable and razor thin.
“The Roommate” is like a female “The Odd Couple” that’s more odd and less funny, and worth a Broadway production for two reasons: Mia Farrow and Patti LuPone.

It’s too bad LuPone’s Robyn is a just a dramatic device to free Farrow’s inner devil—a fuller account of Robyn trying to make good as Sharon turns ever more bad would make The Roommate a better, more intriguing play.

Unfortunately for the purposes of this review, that’s something you’ll have to see the play to find out. Resembling the pilot for an unproduced sitcom about two wacky characters who get into a series of crazy misadventures, the evening proves diverting despite the surprisingly sluggish staging by the normally reliable Jack O’Brien.
One, unfortunately, is the ending.
Not unlike someone you’re forced to live with, it takes up space awkwardly, its good qualities eclipsed by a mounting series of annoyances you cannot overcome.
Despite the slimness of Silverman’s script, her stars, directed with economy and precision by O’Brien, do their best to beef up their scrawny roles.
It is too early in the Broadway season to call something the worst.
It is worth a visit to the Booth Theatre to catch a glimpse of these two actors navigating complex characters and creating some dazzling magic on the Broadway stage.
Still, in the hands of pros like Farrow and LuPone, they manage to glisten just a little bit brighter than the script demands.
The Roommate is a touching reminder that misadventure is not just for young folks and neither is naivety.
Both LuPone and Farrow are still at the top of their game, and that they get better with age and experience.
After her divorce, Sharon needs a housemate for the first time in her life to share her home and expenses in Iowa City.
It’s great to have these acting treasures together on Broadway, even in a so-so, old-fashioned comedy, but it would have been much greater had it been in something of real substance.
The Roommate is a thoroughly disappointing show despite its two star leads.

cn.t: Critics praise Farrow and LuPone's magnetic chemistry in this slight but charming odd-couple comedy, with most finding the stars' performances far more compelling than Silverman's thin, uneven script that strains for both humor and depth.
